## 2. A movie that makes you fall in love with a culture or city

**Score:** 26
**Body:** Two movies come to mind: Rio, and la la land

Rio de Janeiro is probably my favorite city in the world and I just *love* how Rio presents it. Every time I watch it, I wanna book a vacation and go back.

Then on the complete other side: I really don’t like Los Angeles. However, whenever I watch la la land, I feel like it *does* have some very specific magic

I tend to be drawn towards more Latin American cultures, so bonus points if it’s that

## 3. Films like "Drive" with Ryan Gosling.

**Score:** 24
**Body:** Not the plot.  But the atmosphere.  Films that have that sort of almost dreamlike quality with the dreamy New Retro Wave-style music playing throughout.  Also some of it being set at night would be a bonus.

  
EDIT: Thanks for all the great suggestions, I'm watching trailers for all of them even if I don't respond individually.

## 4. Looking for alien movies that focus on science/philosophy rather than action

**Score:** 25
**Body:** Looking for alien first-contact/invasion movies that focus more on the science of encountering aliens and trying to understand/communicate with them rather than fighting them.

* Trying to figure out how the aliens communicate, studying the aliens and figuring out their biology/technology
* The mystery of why they’re here / what they want
* The scientific and logistical problems of making contact
* The political implications of an alien arrival/invasion

I don't mind some action if it's necessary, but I'd prefer little to no fighting/battle sequences. The aliens themselves can be scary or threatening, I just don't want the movie to be mainly an action movie.

The only movie that I've watched with this particular set up is Arrival

1. Contact 

Close encounters of the third kind

Project Hail Mary 
  - Contact never gets old.
2. Arrival
3. Enemy Mine fits this well. 
4. The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951). One of my favorites.
5. K-PAX
6. Annihilation
7. Solaris
8. The Vast of Night 
9. Arrival

Annihilation- requires several watches to really get the whole story

## 5. Looking for a movie with a completely unexpected, jaw-dropping plot twist

**Score:** 24
**Body:** I'm looking for a movie with a plot twist that I genuinely won't see coming—something completely unexpected and jaw-dropping.

I’m open to horror or tense atmospheres, but there are only two things I want to avoid:

\- Jumpscares

\- Movies in languages other than English or Hindi

Atmospheric horror and psychological tension are completely fine. I just don't want any jumpscares.

Hit me with your best recommendations.

## 2. Do you think Dwayne Johnson is no longer the big box office star he once was?

**Score:** 1037
**Body:** Do you think The Rock is washed? The guy used to be one of the biggest box office stars in Hollywood, to the point where his name alone could practically guarantee a movie would be successful. For years, it felt like every major movie he was in was a hit, whether it was *Jumanji*, *Fast & Furious*, *San Andreas*, etc.

But lately, his box-office track record has become pretty questionable. *Black Adam* was a major disappointment with comic book fans, *The Smashing Machine* performed poorly despite getting him a lot of praise for his performance, and now *Moana* seems to be underperforming as well. Obviously, one or two flops don’t mean much, but when you start seeing several of them in a row, it makes you wonder if people are simply getting tired of seeing Dwayne Johnson in everything.

Do you think people have just moved on from The Rock as a box-office draw, or is this just a rough patch and he can still make a comeback?

4. It works for Jason Statham because he embraces the fact that he is not an actor. He just plays himself and he is fine with it. To me it's like the Rock wants too much. He thinks too much of himself. That being said, I absolutely love him in Jumanji!!!

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Does anyone else here miss the slower pacing of movies from the 80's and 90's a ton?

**Score:** 99
**Body:** Watching American Psycho for the first time and it is an absolute joy. While the film was made before my time, there's just something about how it flows together that's just so pleasing to experience in a way that a lot of newer films don't have. Not to say that all newer films are bad nor that movies aren't made like this anymore, I am sure that there are some indie films closer to this style, but there's something about it I'm struggling to describe that I absolutely love.

It gives itself room to breathe, to build things up and do set up and go at an even pace. Watched Memento a while back and felt similar there as well. These are both thrillers, but they take their time without feeling slow at all. It's nice. I feel like if these movies were made today the violence and reveals would be done way earlier and just go go go.

This isn't me complaining about hyper paced 2020's stuff either, and there is plenty of incredible new art being made that I need to get around to. This pacing issue I personally feel I've seen since at least 2015 or so. With the hyper paced super connected world, sitting down and just watching a long form movie with no second screen or distractions or constant notifications is just really nice.

I mean in American Psycho after the first murder Patrick Bateman has blood all over his face, but when he goes to sit down and smoke a cigar the less bloodied side of his face is viewed from the camera. That's an intentional artistic choice, I don't know fully know what it means but I know the artists are trying to say \*something\* without a single line of dialogue.

When the movie Iron Lung came out, a ton of people, including critics, complained about the length and how it was too slow or needed a half hour's worth cut. I could not disagree more. The slow buildup of dread, the feelings of isolation, the uncertainty of if the speaker was working or not by body blocking the wires in the shot thus intentionally making it unclear if the voice on the other end at points was even real, all of that was so well done and intentional and I don't understand how people wouldn't like those details.  
  
I'm glad I have access to all these older titles. I don't have to endlessly complain about new stuff because A. some new art works are being made this way and B. I can easily go back and watch these sorts of things thanks to the largest library in the world being at my fingertips. Who knows, maybe at some point I'll even make something in this style myself. We all have to start somewhere. I don't even necessarily hate newer films either, the second Venom movie had the newer pacing yet despite that the relationship between Eddie and Venom was genuinely heartwarming. I just miss when this pacing and style was more the mainstream and not in more niche spaces is all even having been born after this was the standard. 

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. To me, one of the defining features of films from the 80s through *maybe* as far as the early 2000s was their seconds acts. They take the time to let the story *play* in its narrative. More than anything else, I think that's what tends to make movies that get remembered by most people long term. Too much slavishly chasing after act iii is exhausting on the audience and, when recalled, requires holding the whole structure of the narrative in your head for any quality moments to stand out. 
2. The 1980s?  I miss the pacing of films from the 1950s!

The other night I watched *Gunfight at the O.K. Corral* (1956) and found it utterly enthralling.  Burt Lancaster’s performance in the early barroom confrontation with the drunk brought a packed Geffen Theater to utter silence.
3. Audience habits and trends change. Right now, fast paced films with action, and I think the social media boom had had something to do with it and how it promotes short term dopamine stimulating content. Mainstream American studios are making films in this style because it gets the most people, it in a way appeals to the lowest common denominator.

I didn't even grow up in the 20th century and I think we should return to slower paced films. It's like they don't trust the audience to stay focused.
  - I agree, and I think the trend is going to start shifting back to this style of filming more and more. It's the 20 year cultural churn
  - Is it really the audience habits? The audience doesn't have other options. It's the filmmaking habits changing and the audience being dragged along.
4. I watched Project Hail Mary and was so unimpressed and exhausted by the end due to the frantic edit and the near constant ‘montage mode’ throughout. I was even questioning myself, as everyone else seemed to be enjoying it, am I just miserable?! Then the next day I watched Dog Day Afternoon, a heist film without a soundtrack or any added ambient music, long takes averaging well over a minute per cut. Both concepts completely alien in mainstream filmmaking today, yet the film is so incredibly thrilling and masterful, but not everyone is Sidney Lumet! 
5. Well there's literally a century + of cinema to experience thankfully.

I mean people now don't even watch the thing that's on anymore so I guess we're back to radio days? 

At some point the whole thing will fall apart or become even worse and people will refuse to listen to anybody talking in real life (kinda very much happening already).

So yeah, it's all a life choice ultimately, similar to parents not exposing their kids to social media.
6. I couldn’t agree more. A big thing I have pointed out to my partner that was never into movies when he was younger was how movies from the 80’s to early 2k’s were sometimes just a movie about something, just for the sake of it. 

There was no grand pay off, or big lesson to be learned. It was just a movie about a story, and the process of watching the movie was enjoyable. A good example of this is “fish in the bathtub” 

It’s essentially a a movie about an older couple who’s relationship is tested by them (especially the husband) being stuck in their ways, and you the viewer are along for the ride. 

Ultimately nothing of consequence happens, and it’s just a good time to view it. 
7. I recently watched disclosure day and OG Back to the Future. Seems like Spielberg totally lost it. It was like a big budget X-files double episode but without any of the charm of the series and boring. Action scenes were confusing. Ready Player One wasn't as bad. 

Back to the future was so much better paced, even effects were better. Everything made sense 
8. Kinda the opposite, but actually I think it’s part of the same phenomenon. I miss movies being both tightly paced *and* giving room for exploration/expression. It’s part of why I love early film, so many of those movies are incredibly well planned and well executed in a way that just generally doesn’t happen today. I want those extreme closeups that show every line and twitch on an actors face, dialogue you actually want to pay attention to, and deep visual storytelling, and I want it all in 90 minutes! I love watching a film and being amazed by the composition of shot or wondering how they ever pulled off a bit of trickery or just imagining how many different lights there must be to create a specific visual effect.

## 2. The Movie ‚The Square‘ from 2017 is an example for bystander paralysis. How real are the following aspects?

**Score:** 8
**Body:** The movie depicts a scene of high class individuals all in some form of banquet hall eating and enjoying themselves, when what’s believed to be entertainment shows up. Entertainment in the form of a man acting as an ape.

The thing about this scene is that the actor didn’t know that the people in the room weren’t actors apart from very few. This way it serves as a sociological study of how a group of people acts in face of danger. Most shy away from the situation hoping they won’t get attacked by that ‘ape’. Eventually, they do fight back when a beautiful redheaded woman in a pink gown gets dragged away.

My question is: do you know about what people in the room were real actors that knew about the situation? Was the ape actor actually beaten by the crowd? Did he suffer severe injuries?

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. So I was at the premiere of this. It was at the Fantastic Fest, so Alamo Drafthouse (full food and drink service).

After the movie ended, that dude came barelling in, on the crutches, screaming and knocking plates and glasses off of the bar. It was mayhem and people were truly uncomfortable.

I've been to a lot of interactive screenings; Dawn of the Dead in a mall with zombies and Romero roaming about, for instance. Nothing shook me like that screening.
  - I love that scene! I think is one of my favorite scenes of all times and that guy was awesome. I am so jealous that you got the real life experience, I would have love that. 
2. According to [this article](https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/features/the-square-dinner-ape-scene-terry-notary-ruben-ostlund-a8261266.html), the actor doing the ape impression was not actually beaten or injured by the crowd. The film involved a lot of improvisation and he does say that things got a bit wild, but the scene was shot over multiple days. The crowd wasn’t fully aware of how it would go down, but they weren’t rioting either.
